accuracy.evidence: Claims kept to what the sources support: slow breathing with a longer exhale lowers heart rate through the parasympathetic system (Zaccaro 2018 review; NHS breathing exercise advice), counting adds a pause before acting, and a quiet space removes ongoing triggers. Safety rule that a grown-up must know where the child goes matches school calm-corner guidance. No claim that calming makes a problem vanish.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips parents and teachers report at 5 to 7: fast puffs or breath-holding instead of a slow out-breath (fast puff makes the storm grow in step 1), racing through the count (taps under 600 ms are refused with a reason), running off alone (gate spot), letting it out by hitting or shouting, waiting until the feeling is huge, and thinking calm means the problem is gone.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanics are specific to calming tools: a balloon you drag up and must release slowly (release speed is timed), paced stepping-stone counting with a minimum gap, dragging a child figure into safe versus unsafe spaces, matching a tool to an upset where a loud party needs a quiet space, and a calm-then-fix sequence. It shares no mechanic with the body-alarm dial in flagstress or the body-clue map in flagsoma, and passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step lets the child find the rule by doing: three slow breaths shrink the storm from 4 to 1 while a fast puff pushes it back up; tapping too fast stalls the count; two wrong spots explain why they fail; the loud-party scene shows that breathing alone does not stop noise; and the order step refuses 'fix it' until the body has settled, which is the 'calm helps you think' idea from the topic evidence.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: fast puffs vs slow breaths out, counting as a magic word vs giving the body time, running out of the gate to be alone vs a safe quiet place, and 'the problem is all gone' once Leo is calm. The done message restates the learner's choice and why it was right or wrong.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions rotate answer order. Thirteen distinct m= messages name the slip: hitting or yelling makes the storm bigger, fast puffs speed the heart, holding the breath makes you tight, all feelings are OK but hitting is not, going off alone is unsafe, noise keeps the body buzzing, a huge storm is hardest so notice early, calming does not fix the problem or win the game.

readability.evidence: Kid text measured FK 0.6 against the family limit of 5.0, with short sentences and concrete images (balloon, hot soup, big steps, calm corner). Adult text measured FK 9.8 against 10.0; it explains the stress response in plain terms. Canvas labels are two or three words and wrap inside their boxes on a 360 px screen.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and 12% duplication gates against all 239 lessons. Each kid paragraph teaches one tool or rule, each adult paragraph covers the goal, the mechanism, the named mistakes or the lab, and the family tip gives one concrete routine (bedtime breaths and an agreed calm spot).

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360x640 Android and iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark: the young class gives 56 px buttons, every canvas card has a matching button, tool and order labels wrap to two lines instead of clipping (fixed after the first screenshot pass showed 'Use a calm tool' cut off), and the phone sweep reported 0 findings.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone in the walkthrough. Every drag (balloon, Mia) and tap target has a labelled button alternative, the canvas aria-label reads the live storm size, count and choices, and success is shown by text as well as colour.
